title: How the Navajo Code Talkers Worked
summary: Josh and Chuck explain the Navajo code talkers of World War Two, who spoke their Navajo language to send unbreakable, fast tactical messages in the Pacific Theater. They cover Navajo history (the Long Walk, forced boarding schools and language bans), earlier Choctaw, Comanche and other Native code talkers in World War One, Philip Johnston's proposal and recruitment of about 29 original Navajo speakers, how the code-within-a-code worked (three words per letter, imagery, compound word substitutions), key battles including Guadalcanal and Iwo Jima, postwar neglect, and later recognition. The episode ends with a listener mail story about an Easy Bake oven.

segments.title: Opening banter and episode introduction
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about bad French onion soup and soup restaurants, then introduce the episode on Navajo code talkers, noting other tribes also served and that the Wind Talkers movie is not a good portrayal.

segments.title: Navajo history and the Long Walk
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Navajo's settlement in the Southwest, conflicts with the Spanish and other tribes, the forced Long Walk to New Mexico, and the later U.S. government policy of forced assimilation through boarding schools and language bans.

segments.title: World War One code talkers and Germany's response
segments.summary: In World War One, Choctaw soldiers were used to relay messages in their native tongue after a captain heard them speaking. Comanche and other tribes also played roles. Germany later studied Native American languages in the United States, which compromised their use before World War Two. Native World War One code talkers were not recognized by the U.S. until 2008, and France recognized them first.

segments.title: Philip Johnston proposes Navajo code talkers
segments.summary: Philip Johnston, a white man raised on a Navajo reservation who was a World War One veteran, proposed a Navajo code team. He demonstrated with four Navajo men recruited in Los Angeles at Camp Elliott, and the method was adopted.

segments.title: Recruitment, training and the Navajo language
segments.summary: Johnston recruited young Navajo men from reservations; about 29 original code talkers were used to create the code, and 400-plus served. The Navajo language's tonal complexity made it extremely hard for outsiders, and non-Navajo speakers failed the program.

segments.title: How the code within a code worked
segments.summary: The Navajo code talkers used Navajo code words, three different words for each letter for spelling, imagery-based words for military terms, and compound substitutions such as dispatch being rendered as dog and patch. Words for things missing in Navajo were invented, and the code was never written down.

segments.title: Battles and wartime impact
segments.summary: Code talkers served at Guadalcanal and Iwo Jima, sending over 800 messages without error in the first 48 hours at Iwo Jima. Major Howard Conner said the Marines might not have taken Iwo Jima without them. Navajo speakers were sometimes mistaken for Japanese by American soldiers, and George McCabe was briefly detained at Guadalcanal.

segments.title: Postwar treatment, recognition and honors
segments.summary: After the war the program stayed classified until 1968 and code talkers returned to reservation poverty. GI Bill home loans were blocked because reservation land was held in trust. Nixon gave a certificate in 1971, National Code Talker Day was set in 2014 (August 14), a Congressional Gold Medal was given, and Chester Nez, the last original code talker, died in 2014.

segments.title: Kayenta museum tip
segments.summary: Josh suggests that a Burger King in Kayenta, Arizona has a small Navajo code talker display.

segments.title: Listener mail: Easy Bake oven
segments.summary: A listener from Portland, Oregon, Davina H. M Berry, shares a story about her son choosing an Easy Bake oven with his birthday money and insisting on carrying it home.
